items.prompt: What does a manual check actually verify?
choices: Every input the code will ever receive from users
That later changes elsewhere cannot break the feature
One run, with the inputs tried, at the moment it was tried
That nothing else in the codebase has a bug
items.explanation: A manual check is a snapshot: it covers the specific run that was observed and nothing beyond it.

items.prompt: You checked the kitchen light before leaving and it was off. What does that tell you about the garage light?
choices: Nothing, because you never looked at it
It is probably off too, since the kitchen was
It is off because lights are normally switched together
It is on, because you only notice lights that are on
items.explanation: A check says nothing about things it did not look at. The garage was outside the route.

items.prompt: A feature worked when you clicked through it two weeks ago. Does that alone show it works today?
choices: Yes, because working code stays working
Yes, as long as you were careful two weeks ago
Only if nobody has said anything is wrong
No
items.explanation: The check is two weeks old. Any change since then is invisible to it.

items.prompt: What is a regression?
choices: A feature that was never finished or never worked
Something that worked before stops working after a change
A change that makes a page load more slowly in general
A planned removal of an old feature by the team
items.explanation: A regression is breakage of previously working behavior, often caused by a change somewhere else.

items.prompt: What is an automated test in one line?
choices: A check that only the original author is able to run
A check saved as a script that can be re-run on demand
A check that proves the code has no bugs at all
A check done by hand but written up afterwards in a report
items.explanation: The check is written down as something runnable, so repeating it costs almost nothing.

items.prompt: A manual check depends on which of these every time it is repeated?
choices: A script that is saved alongside the code
A machine that runs the steps unattended
A report listing results of earlier runs
A person remembering and performing the steps
items.explanation: Manual means a human does it again, so it is only as repeatable as that person's time and memory.

items.prompt: In the light analogy, what plays the part of the checklist that runs itself?
choices: An automated test suite that re-runs on every change
The person who walks through the house by hand
A note on the fridge saying all lights are fine
The kitchen light that you happened to check
items.explanation: The suite is the written-down walk-through that runs without a person.

items.prompt: Your friend says "it passed when I tried it". Which claim does that support?
choices: It works for every input
It will work after the next change
It worked then, for what was tried
It works in every part of the product
items.explanation: The statement is true but narrow: it covers what was tried and when.

items.prompt: A developer clicks through a form with three typical inputs and all three work. Which is the strongest claim that check supports?
choices: The form handles every valid input that a user may type
The form will keep working after next month's changes land
The form handled those three inputs correctly at that moment
No other page in the product depends on the form's code
items.explanation: The check observed three runs at one moment. Every other claim reaches past what was observed.
items.reference:
A check is a snapshot
checked: this input, this moment
not covered: other inputs, other callers
not covered: tomorrow's code
automated test: the same check, re-runnable
Why: a snapshot proves what was looked at, once; only a repeatable check can say anything about later.
items.learnMore:
A manual check is a snapshot

It answers one question: did this specific thing work, for these inputs, right now? Whether it still works after unrelated code changes is a different question that the snapshot cannot answer.

Common mistake

Reading a passing check as a statement about the whole system instead of the part that was looked at.
items.reflection: Think of a habit where you checked something once and assumed it stayed fine. What changed afterwards that your check could not have seen?

items.prompt: On Monday one teammate reports a passing manual check. On Friday, after twelve more changes landed, another teammate reports one too. Which report says more about Friday's code?
choices: Friday's, though only for the inputs that person tried
Monday's, since earlier checks tend to be more careful ones
Both equally, because a pass is a pass whatever the day
Neither, since a manual pass never says anything about code
items.explanation: Friday's check ran against the current code, so it is relevant, but it is still limited to what that person tried.

items.prompt: A team replaces its click-through before release with a script that performs the same clicks and compares the results. What is the main thing that changed?
choices: The script now covers inputs the old clicking never reached
The check now proves the application contains no bugs
The check no longer depends on anyone choosing what to try
The same inputs can be re-run on every change at no effort
items.explanation: Automation makes the same check cheap to repeat. Someone still chose the inputs, so coverage is unchanged.

items.prompt: A shared function is used by three features. A developer changes it while working on one feature. How many features can the change affect?
choices: Only the one being worked on
All three
Only the two that were not being worked on
None unless the function's name changes
items.explanation: Shared code serves every feature that calls it, so a change reaches all of them.

items.prompt: Why did the developer in the example miss the refund tool?
choices: They were lazy and skipped the final check
They did not know the refund tool used the function
The refund tool was too slow to test by hand
The pricing function was written in a different language
items.explanation: The gap was knowledge of the dependency, not effort.

items.prompt: Which part of a manual check is limited by what the person knows?
choices: How quickly the person can click
How many monitors the person has
Whether the person likes the feature
Choosing which places to re-check
items.explanation: A person can only pick places they know about.

items.prompt: Extra diligence mostly improves checking of which places?
choices: The places the person already knows about
Places the person has never heard of
Places in other teams' unrelated products
Places that have no connection to the change
items.explanation: Diligence deepens checks of known places. It cannot reveal unknown ones.

items.prompt: What does a saved suite of checks re-run?
choices: Only the checks for the file that changed
Only the checks the developer picks that day
Every saved check, even forgotten ones
Only the checks written in the last week
items.explanation: The suite does not depend on anyone's memory of what is connected.

items.prompt: What does "indirectly affected" code mean?
choices: Code you edited but whose behavior stayed the same
Code that only exists in the documentation files
Code that depends on what you changed, though you did not edit it
Code that was deleted during the same change
items.explanation: Indirect effects travel through dependencies, not through edits.

items.prompt: A suite has a check for the refund behavior. A change breaks refunds. When does the team find out?
choices: When the suite runs, before the change ships
When a customer opens a support ticket
When the next quarterly audit takes place
When the developer remembers the refund tool
items.explanation: A saved check fails at run time, which is before shipping if the suite runs on each change.

items.prompt: Which statement matches the garage-light lesson?
choices: Garage lights are always the first place to look
Checking more slowly finds every hidden light
Hidden lights never matter if the kitchen is fine
You can only re-check what you know to look at
items.explanation: The lesson is about visibility: unknown places go unchecked.

items.prompt: A developer is extremely careful and re-checks all five places they know use a shared function. It actually has seven callers. What is the outcome?
choices: All seven are now covered because five were checked well
The two callers they did not know about remain unchecked
The two unknown callers are covered by the careful checks
The two unknown callers cannot be affected by the change
items.explanation: Care cannot extend to callers the developer cannot see. Two stay unchecked.
items.reference:
One change, many callers
shared function changed
known caller: re-checked by hand
unknown callers: not re-checked
saved checks: re-run for every caller
Why: care improves checks of the places you know; it cannot reach places you do not know exist.
items.learnMore:
Visibility, not effort

A change to shared code can affect every place that uses it, but a person can only re-check the places they remember. A suite of saved checks re-runs all of them, including ones nobody thinks of at the moment of the change.

Common mistake

Believing a more diligent person would have caught it. The blocker was what the person could see, not how hard they tried.
items.reflection: Think of a shared resource, like a template or a shared spreadsheet. Who else depends on it that you might never think to ask before changing it?

items.prompt: A team's habit is to re-test whichever files they edited. They edit a shared helper in a library folder. What is the biggest gap in that habit?
choices: Edited files are always too large to test in a reasonable time
Files that call the helper were not edited, so they get no re-test
The helper itself can never be tested by anyone at all
Library folders are tested by other companies before release
items.explanation: Edit-based re-testing misses callers, which is exactly where indirect breakage appears.

items.prompt: After the refund incident, the team adds a saved check for the refund behavior. What does it protect against specifically?
choices: A repeat of the incident but only when the same developer returns
Every possible bug in the pricing function and all its callers
Any problem in the support ticket process that found the bug
Any later change, even by someone unaware of the refund tool
items.explanation: The check records the dependency once, so it guards against later changes regardless of who makes them.

items.prompt: Assume writing a check takes 15 minutes once and each manual re-check takes 3 minutes. After how many manual re-checks have the two routes cost the same?
items.explanation: 15 divided by 3 is 5. After the fifth manual re-check the manual route has cost as much.

items.prompt: Which cost is paid only once?
choices: Re-checking by hand after each change
Remembering what to re-check each time
Writing the automated check
Walking through the product after a change
items.explanation: The check is written once. The manual costs repeat.

items.prompt: A product has 20 flows and one hand re-check of a flow takes 3 minutes. How long does a full manual re-check take?
choices: 23 minutes
17 minutes
60 minutes
6 minutes
items.explanation: 20 flows times 3 minutes is 60 minutes.

items.prompt: Which cost repeats on every change when you re-check by hand?
choices: A person's time
The one-time writing of a test
The price of the code editor
The size of the repository
items.explanation: Each manual re-check consumes a person's time again.

items.prompt: Why does speed matter for a check?
choices: Fast checks are always more accurate than slow ones
Slow checks cannot find any bugs at all
Speed only matters for the people who write the checks
Cheap checks run on every change, costly ones rarely
items.explanation: How often a check is actually run depends on how cheap it is.

items.prompt: When does writing a test not pay off?
choices: When the code is used by many other features
When the code is touched once and never again
When the code changes a few times every week
When the code is important to the company
items.explanation: Without repeat runs there is nothing for the one-time cost to be spread over.

items.prompt: With 3 minutes per manual re-check, how many total minutes do 10 changes cost by hand?
items.explanation: 10 changes times 3 minutes each is 30 minutes.

items.prompt: A product grows from 20 flows to 40 flows. What happens to the time for one full manual re-check?
choices: It stays the same
It grows by only a few minutes
It drops by half
It doubles
items.explanation: Cost per flow is fixed, so twice the flows takes twice the time.

items.prompt: Writing a check takes 15 minutes once and a manual re-check takes 3 minutes. The code is expected to change 12 more times. Which statement is right?
choices: The written check is cheaper by 21 minutes (15 against 36)
The manual route is cheaper by 21 minutes (15 against 36)
The two routes cost the same, meeting at exactly 12 changes
The written check is cheaper by 6 minutes (30 against 36)
items.explanation: 12 manual re-checks cost 36 minutes against 15 once, a saving of 21 minutes.
items.reference:
A one-time cost against a repeating one
write the check once: 15 minutes (assumed)
manual re-check each change: 3 minutes (assumed)
break-even: 15 / 3 = 5 changes
after that the gap only widens
Why: a repeating cost always overtakes a one-time cost if the code keeps changing.
items.learnMore:
Why frequency decides

Writing a check costs time now, while skipping it costs nothing today but a re-check on every later change. The only case where skipping wins is code that is touched once and never again.

Common mistake

Judging a test by the cost of writing it alone, ignoring how many times it will be run.
items.reflection: Think of a chore you could automate or keep doing by hand. How often does it repeat, and where is your break-even point?

items.prompt: A product has 40 flows at 3 minutes each and ships 4 changes a day. What happens in practice?
choices: Full re-checking takes only 2 hours a day, so it always gets done
The team hires more testers until every flow is always re-checked
Full re-checking takes 8 hours, so only touched areas get re-checked
Each flow takes less time to check as the product grows
items.explanation: 40 times 3 times 4 is 480 minutes. At that cost people quietly narrow to the touched area.

items.prompt: A throwaway script will be written, run once, and deleted the same day. What is the rational choice?
choices: Write a full suite for it, since every script deserves tests
Skip checking entirely, since deleted code cannot have bugs
Check it by hand once, as a saved test would never repay itself
Write the saved test, since writing is always cheaper than checking
items.explanation: A one-time cost only pays back through repeated runs. One run means no payback.

items.prompt: What gives a test its value?
choices: An independently correct expected value
The number of lines in the test file
The test using the newest testing tools
The test running on a very fast machine
items.explanation: A test only protects you if its expected value is known to be right on its own.

items.prompt: Which test can never fail? expect(f(2)).toBe(f(2))
choices: It uses a number that is too small to be useful
It calls the function with an argument of the wrong type
It forgets to import the testing library it needs
It compares the function's output with its own output
items.explanation: Both sides come from the same function, so they are always equal.

items.prompt: What is a flaky test?
choices: One that always fails on a certain day
One that passes and fails with no change to the code
One that takes more than a second to finish
One that tests only the happiest path
items.explanation: Flakiness means the result depends on something other than the code's correctness.

items.prompt: What happens to a team that re-runs the suite until it turns green?
choices: The suite becomes more accurate over time
Real failures start to look like the usual noise
Flaky tests fix themselves after enough runs
The code under test improves with each re-run
items.explanation: When failures are routinely ignored, a real one gets ignored too.

items.prompt: A test checks that an internal helper was called, not what the result is. What does it pin?
choices: What the code does for its users
Which version of the language is used
Whether the code has been reviewed
How the code works, not what it does
items.explanation: It describes the implementation, so it breaks when the implementation changes.

items.prompt: Do automated tests discover which behaviors matter by themselves?
choices: No, someone has to identify and write them down
Yes, they find every important behavior on their own
Yes, once the suite has enough tests in it
Only when the tests are written in a certain order
items.explanation: A suite only checks what someone chose to record.

items.prompt: After a refactor that kept behavior identical, many tests fail. What does that suggest?
choices: The refactor must have introduced new bugs
The tests are too fast to be accurate
The tests are tied to implementation details
The tests were never run before the refactor
items.explanation: Behavior-focused tests survive behavior-preserving changes.

items.prompt: What should a good failing test tell you?
choices: Only that something somewhere is wrong
Which developer wrote the code last
Which specific check failed and what was expected
How many tests exist in the whole suite
items.explanation: Specificity is a big part of a test's value: it points at the cause.

items.prompt: Which single test would catch the 150-percent change that capped discounts at 100?
choices: expect(applyDiscount(100, 150)).toBe(-50)
expect(applyDiscount(100, 20)).toBe(80)
expect(typeof applyDiscount(100, 150)).toBe("number")
expect(applyDiscount(100, 150) <= 100).toBeTruthy()
items.explanation: Only the 150 case with the original result of -50 differs after the cap. The other three pass both before and after.
items.reference:
When a green suite means something
expected value correct on its own: real check
output compared with itself: cannot fail
fails with no code change: flaky
breaks on behavior-preserving refactor: pins the how
Why: a suite earns trust only when a failure means something and silence means the behaviors really are checked.
items.learnMore:
Trust is the product

Tests only protect you if people believe their results. Checks that cannot fail, fail randomly, or fail on harmless refactors teach the team to ignore or delete them, which removes the protection.

Common mistake

Counting tests rather than asking whether each one could actually fail for a real reason.
items.reflection: Think of an alarm, a warning light or a notification you learned to ignore. What made it stop being trustworthy, and what would restore that trust?

items.prompt: A suite fails about one run in ten with no code change, and the team re-runs it until it passes. What is the hidden cost?
choices: The suite stops running tests that failed once before
Passing runs get slower because of the extra attempts
Every later run becomes flaky as a direct result
A real failure gets mistaken for the usual noise
items.explanation: Once a red result is treated as probably noise, a real regression gets the same treatment.

items.prompt: A harmless internal rename leaves behavior unchanged, yet 14 tests fail because they assert the order of internal calls. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: The rename broke 14 separate behaviors that need fixing
The tests pin internal steps, not what the code returns
The tests are correct and the rename should be undone
The suite needs more tests so the failures get diluted
items.explanation: Failures with unchanged behavior mean the tests described the implementation. Asserting outputs removes the coupling.

items.prompt: Implement `isPass(actual, expected)`: return true when the two values are the same, otherwise false. Use `Object.is`.
items.explanation: Object.is compares two values and returns true or false, which is exactly a pass or a fail.

items.prompt: Implement `countPassing(results)`: `results` is an array of booleans. Return how many are true.
items.explanation: Keeping only the true entries and taking the length counts the passing checks.

items.prompt: Implement `allPass(results)`: return true only when every entry in the array of booleans is true. An empty array counts as all passing.
items.explanation: A suite is green only if no entry is false. With nothing in it, nothing failed.

items.prompt: Implement `anyFailing(results)`: return true when at least one entry in the array of booleans is false.
items.explanation: A single false entry means the suite is red.

items.prompt: Implement `failCount(results)`: return how many entries in the array of booleans are false.
items.explanation: Counting the false entries tells you how many checks no longer hold.

items.prompt: Implement `runCase(fn, args, expected)`: call `fn` with the values in `args` and return true when the result equals `expected` (use `Object.is`).
items.explanation: A case is data: inputs and an expected result. Running it means calling the function and comparing.

items.prompt: Implement `firstFailure(names, results)`: `names` and `results` have the same length. Return the name of the first entry whose result is false, or null if none.
items.explanation: The index of the first false result points at the matching name.

items.prompt: Implement `failingNames(cases)`: each case is `{ name, passed }`. Return the names of the cases where `passed` is false, in order.

tests.expr: expect(failingNames([{ name: "a", passed: true }, { name: "b", passed: false }])).toEqual(["b"])
expect(failingNames([{ name: "x", passed: false }, { name: "y", passed: false }])).toEqual(["x", "y"])

items.explanation: Filtering on the failing flag and mapping to names produces a readable report of what broke.

items.prompt: Implement `failingCases(fn, cases)`. Each case is `{ name, args, expected }`. Call `fn` with the values in `args` and return the names of the cases whose result is not the same as `expected` (use `Object.is`), in order. An empty list of cases fails nothing.

tests.expr: expect(failingCases((a, b) => a - a * (b / 100), [{ name: "normal", args: [100, 20], expected: 80 }, { name: "refund over 100", args: [100, 150], expected: -50 }])).toEqual([])

expect(failingCases((a, b) => a - a * (Math.min(b, 100) / 100), [{ name: "normal", args: [100, 20], expected: 80 }, { name: "refund over 100", args: [100, 150], expected: -50 }])).toEqual(["refund over 100"])

items.explanation: Each case is a recorded fact. The runner calls the function and keeps the names of cases that no longer hold, so the capped version is flagged by name.
items.reference:
A suite is a list of cases plus a runner
case: name, inputs, expected result
runner: call the function on each case
report: names of cases that no longer hold
written once, re-run on every change
Why: the dependency is recorded as data the first time, so later changes are checked against it without anyone remembering.
items.learnMore:
Recording a fact once

Each case writes down one thing that must stay true. The runner compares what the function returns with what was recorded and reports the names of the mismatches.

Common mistake

Forgetting that Object.is-style equality means -0 and 0 differ and NaN equals NaN. Keep expected values plain numbers or strings.
items.reflection: Think of a rule your team keeps in someone's head. How would you write it down as a case that anyone can run?

items.prompt: Implement `countFailing(fn, cases)`. Each case is `{ name, args, expected }`. Return how many cases have a result from `fn(...args)` that is not the same as `expected` (use `Object.is`).

tests.expr: expect(countFailing((n) => n % 2 === 0, [{ name: "four", args: [4], expected: true }, { name: "seven", args: [7], expected: false }])).toBe(0)
expect(countFailing((n) => n % 2 === 1, [{ name: "four", args: [4], expected: false }, { name: "seven", args: [7], expected: false }, { name: "two", args: [2], expected: true }])).toBe(2)

items.explanation: The runner is a loop over recorded cases. Each mismatch adds one to the count, which tells you how much of the recorded behavior no longer holds.
items.reference:
A suite is a list of cases plus a runner
case: name, inputs, expected result
runner: call the function on each case
report: names of cases that no longer hold
written once, re-run on every change
Why: the dependency is recorded as data the first time, so later changes are checked against it without anyone remembering.

Each case writes down one thing that must stay true. The runner compares what the function returns with what was recorded and reports the names of the mismatches.

Common mistake

Forgetting that Object.is-style equality means -0 and 0 differ and NaN equals NaN. Keep expected values plain numbers or strings.
items.reflection: Think of a rule your team keeps in someone's head. How would you write it down as a case that anyone can run?

items.prompt: Implement `firstFailing(fn, cases)`. Each case is `{ name, args, expected }`. Return the name of the first case whose result is not the same as `expected` (use `Object.is`), or `null` if every case holds.

tests.expr: expect(firstFailing((s) => s.toLowerCase(), [{ name: "lower", args: ["ab"], expected: "ab" }, { name: "upper", args: ["AB"], expected: "AB" }, { name: "mixed", args: ["Ab"], expected: "AB" }])).toBe("upper")

items.explanation: Stopping at the first mismatch gives the quickest pointer to what broke, and returning null signals that every recorded case still holds.
items.reference:
A suite is a list of cases plus a runner
case: name, inputs, expected result
runner: call the function on each case
report: names of cases that no longer hold
written once, re-run on every change
Why: the dependency is recorded as data the first time, so later changes are checked against it without anyone remembering.
items.learnMore:
Recording a fact once

Each case writes down one thing that must stay true. The runner compares what the function returns with what was recorded and reports the names of the mismatches.

Common mistake

Forgetting that Object.is-style equality means -0 and 0 differ and NaN equals NaN. Keep expected values plain numbers or strings.
items.reflection: Think of a rule your team keeps in someone's head. How would you write it down as a case that anyone can run?
